probes.query: Why can't the write-ahead log simply be truncated up to the most recent committed entry, and what decides the safe cut point?
expectedFacts: Pre-writes of uncommitted transactions are not persisted in the main store, so their Raft entries must be kept until the transaction commits or aborts.

calculateSnapshot scans entries and sets the snapshot index just before the first mutation whose start ts is at or above the minimum pending start ts; the minimum is the smaller of the Oracle's MinPendingStartTs and the CDC tracker's oldest unsent ts.
The snapshot's ReadTs is the maximum commit timestamp seen; no snapshot is made if nothing can be discarded.
probes.author: r3-dgraph-drafter
probes.notes: VERIFICATION: worker/draft.go:1728-1756 doc comment and signature (MUST keep all pending transactions in the Raft logs at 1736; 'we don't persist pre-writes to disk in pstore' at 1734-1735); :1845-1851 `start >= minPendingStart && snapshotIdx == 0 -> snapshotIdx = entry.Index - 1`; :1852-1856 maxCommitTs; :1135 `minPendingStart := x.Min(posting.Oracle().MinPendingStartTs(), n.cdcTracker.getTs())`; :1879-1884 skip if insufficient entries; posting/oracle.go:243-254 MinPendingStartTs.

probes.query: When I let jj search history for the first commit that breaks my test script, how is each commit's exit code translated into a verdict, and which component chooses the next commit to try?
expectedFacts: evaluate_commit checks out the candidate commit, runs the command, and maps exit status 0 to Good, 125 to Skip, 127 (command not found) to Abort, and any other nonzero code to Bad.

Bisector::next_step first returns any pending precondition verifications; otherwise it evaluates candidates().bisect().latest(1), where the candidates are the input range between the good heads and bad roots, minus bad and skipped commits.
Skipped commits are removed from the candidate set, and the result can be FoundDespiteSkips when skipped commits sit between good and bad.

probes.query: A query block asks for only the first few results, possibly with a skip offset. Sometimes the storage read itself stops early; sometimes everything is read and trimmed afterwards. What decides which, and after how many entries does the storage read stop?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: calculatePaginationParams (query/query.go) pushes count and offset into the storage query only if the block has no filter, no ordering, a non-zero count, and its source function is not one of the multi-token string matchers (regular expression, all-of-terms, all-of-text, fuzzy match, n-gram).

Otherwise it asks for the maximum count with offset 0, so the whole list is read and the count and offset are applied afterwards in the query layer (applyPagination, or the ordering path for blocks with an order).

CRITICAL: On the worker, uidReadFirst (worker/task.go) turns a positive pushed-down count into count plus max(offset, 0) entries to read; zero or the maximum value means read everything, and a negative count is passed through without adding the offset.
Bounded reads also disable uid precalculation for the key (shouldPrecalculateUids returns false when the read is bounded), so those lists are not materialized into the cache.

probes.query: When an install or update is interrupted, either by a failure or by a termination request from the operating system, which separate pieces of leftover state does Composer clean up, and which component does each one? Give the trigger and each distinct cleanup action.

FileDownloader::cleanup deletes the downloaded archive file, removes any extra registered cleanup paths, and removes the package directory, the vendor/<vendor> directory, vendor/composer and the vendor directory when each is empty and is not the current working directory.

ArchiveDownloader::install defines a local cleanup closure run when extraction fails: it clears the cache entry written for the file, removes the temporary extraction directory and the target path (unless it is the current directory) and unregisters those cleanup paths.

ArchiveDownloader::cleanup records that cleanup was executed for the package, and ZipDownloader's system-unzip failure handler checks that record and throws 'installation was aborted by another package operation' instead of falling back to ZipArchive.
CRITICAL: VcsDownloader::cleanup, on an 'update' where local changes were stashed in prepare, re-applies those changes to the checkout (reapplyChanges) and forgets the stash marker.

probes.query: A site enables two bundled request-rewriting plugins: one that tidies repeated and trailing path separators and is set to answer with a redirect instead of rewriting silently, and one that forces encrypted transport and has no alternative secure host configured. A client sends an unencrypted request for a path with doubled and trailing separators, plus a query string. Which chain of code produces the single reply the client gets? Start where the framework first lets plugin code intercept the request, and say what status and location the reply carries.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Redirector::initAndStart registers one synchronous advice with the framework. HttpServer::onRequests calls the static passSyncAdvices in HttpServer.cc, which calls AopAdvice::passSyncAdvices before routing. A non-null response from that advice is sent and the request is not routed.

SlashRemover::initAndStart registers its handleReq function as a path-rewrite handler (not a forward handler) because redirect is on. handleReq collapses the doubled and trailing separators with setPath.
The Redirector advice runs all path-rewrite handlers first, then all redirect handlers. So the secure-transport handler sees the already-rewritten path.
SecureSSLRedirector::redirectToSSL sets the protocol to https:// and leaves the host empty when no secure host is configured and the request has a Host header.

CRITICAL: Redirector builds the location from the protocol, the request's Host header, the rewritten path, and '?' plus the original query. It returns HttpResponse::newRedirectionResponse(url) whose default status is 302 Found.
The client therefore gets one 302 reply to the https URL with the cleaned path (for example //docs//a/ becomes /docs/a), not two redirects.

probes.query: In a database with several reader connections, what makes sure a reader never goes back into the pool of reusable readers while it is still inside an open read transaction, or else is thrown away instead of reused? Name each safeguard and where it lives.
expectedFacts: DatabasePool.init forces allowsUnsafeTransactions = false on the reader configuration, whatever the user configured, because the same reader may not be obtained again to close a dangling transaction (DatabasePool.swift:56-63; Configuration.swift:278-282).

CRITICAL: SerializedDatabase.preconditionNoUnsafeTransactionLeft is a fatal precondition run (via defer) at the end of sync, reentrantSync, async and async execute accesses; it fails if the connection is still inside a transaction, unless an override or the configuration allows it (SerializedDatabase.swift:131, 142, 197-234, 261, 297-309).

Synchronous DatabasePool.read runs the user closure inside Database.isolated, which opens a savepoint (a real transaction when outermost) and commits it when the closure returns (DatabasePool.swift:339-352; Database.swift:1569-1597).
The async read paths begin a deferred transaction and use a defer that tries commit and falls back to rollback before the reader is released with .reuse (DatabasePool.swift:354-379, 381-415).

CRITICAL: For long-lived snapshot reads, walSnapshotTransaction and asyncWALSnapshotTransaction release the reader with .discard instead of .reuse when it is still inside a transaction, and WALSnapshotTransaction.commitAndRelease tries hard to leave the transaction first; Pool.release removes a discarded reader from the pool (DatabasePool.swift:694-700, 716-723; WALSnapshotTransaction.swift:13-27; Pool.swift:165-175).

probes.query: An application interceptor swaps in a different pool of reusable connections for just one call. Which pool supplies and receives the connection that call uses, and which pool is told when the call ends and its connection becomes idle? Do these differ, and what is the consequence?
expectedFacts: RealInterceptorChain.withConnectionPool returns a chain copy with the override and is allowed only before an exchange exists (check(exchange == null)), so a network interceptor gets an IllegalStateException.

RealCall.enterNetworkInterceptorExchange builds the RealRoutePlanner with chain.connectionPool.delegate, so pooled-connection lookups (callAcquirePooledConnection) use the override pool, and ConnectPlan.handleSuccess puts a newly made connection into that same pool (connectionPool.put) which schedules its cleanup.

CRITICAL: RealCall keeps a private connectionPool field initialised once from client.connectionPool.delegate, and releaseConnectionNoEvents calls that field's connectionBecameIdle(connection) when the call's last use ends; so the idle notification goes to the client's own pool, not the override pool.

CRITICAL: Consequence: the client pool's connectionBecameIdle will, if the connection has noNewExchanges or the client pool's maxIdleConnections is 0, mark it noNewExchanges, try to remove it (a no-op there) and return true so RealCall closes the socket even though it lives in the override pool; otherwise it only schedules the client pool's cleanup and returns false. The override pool is never told and relies on its own cleanup task.

probes.query: Several code paths in the model layer fetch one row by its primary key value: the model class's subscript form, a class-level finder method, a dataset-level finder, and an instance reload. In a standard model whose table is a plain table name and whose primary key is a single column, which one runs when application code looks a record up through the class's subscript form with a single key value, how does it build its SELECT, and in which configurations does it fall back to a general first-row query?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Model.[] with a non-hash argument calls primary_key_lookup (hash arguments go to first).

CRITICAL: primary_key_lookup, when @fast_pk_lookup_sql is set, duplicates that prefix string, appends the literalized key with literal_append and runs fetch_rows, returning the first row through the dataset's row_proc (no LIMIT clause); otherwise it calls dataset.first(primary_key_hash(pk)).
@fast_pk_lookup_sql is the string 'SELECT * FROM <table> WHERE <pk> = ' built by reset_fast_pk_lookup_sql, only when both @simple_table and @simple_pk are set.

@simple_table is set by convert_input_dataset for a symbol/identifier/qualified identifier, or for a dataset that is a simple select-all (unset for aliased/literal sources and joined datasets), and @simple_pk by set_primary_key only for a single non-array key.
set_dataset clears the fast SQL when the dataset does not support placeholder literalizers, and the sql_comments plugin disables it by overriding reset_fast_pk_lookup_sql.

The look-alike paths differ: Dataset#with_pk uses a cached placeholder-literalizer loader with a table-qualified condition and LIMIT 1, Model.with_pk delegates to primary_key_lookup, and Model#refresh's _refresh_get uses the fast SQL unless the dataset has a lock style.
